context: Arachne hangs from the stone. She is making a big web. She does not finish it. Instead, she cuts the web right in the middle. She makes two parts to show you the structure is divided. This is the definition: The word "cleft" means divided.
narrative: Arachne hangs from the stone. She is making a big web. She does not finish it. Instead, she cuts the web right in the middle. She makes two parts to show you the structure is divided. This is the definition: The word "cleft" means divided.

narrative: Next to her, a Bird of Paradise opens its colorful feathers. It wants you to look at a passport on the ground. It hits a fake passport to fix the mistake. It makes a loud noise at a traveler. The bird says: "Her passport? No. It was my passport that she dropped." This shows why we use cleft sentences: For Emphasis and Correction.

context: Down the street, a Cat sits on a government paper. You try to move the cat, but it stays there. It shows that this is the paper you need. The cat says: "It's form B6115 that you need." This shows the It-Cleft Structure: It plus "to be" plus
narrative: A Dragon goes to a party. Mickey and Minnie Mouse are the hosts. The hosts are plural (two people). But the Dragon uses fire to make them use a singular verb. He shouts: "It is Matt and Jessica who are having the party, not me." The rule is: Use the singular "Be," even for plural subjects.

context: High up, an Eagle holds a famous book in its claws. It shouts the name of the author to everyone below. "I believe it was Shel Silverstein who wrote The Giving Tree." The Eagle shows you the Relative Pronouns: Who or That.
narrative: Go to the second street.

context: A Frog watches words fly by. It sees a "Subject" and a "Verb." Then it sees the word "that." The word "that" acts as an object. The Frog uses its tongue to catch and eat the word. The rule is: If you have a subject and a verb after your rel
narrative: A Frog watches words fly by. It sees a "Subject" and a "Verb." Then it sees the word "that." The word "that" acts as an object. The Frog uses its tongue to catch and eat the word. The rule is: If you have a subject and a verb after your relative pronoun, you can take it out.

context: A Goat chews on an empty wallet. It shouts loudly. It says the "Wh-clause"—the thing "What we need"—must be money. It cries: "What we need is more money." This shows the Wh-Cleft Structure.
narrative: A Goat chews on an empty wallet. It shouts loudly. It says the "Wh-clause"—the thing "What we need"—must be money. It cries: "What we need is more money." This shows the Wh-Cleft Structure.

context: The Hydra holds a heavy car battery in its main head. It moves the battery all the way to its tail. It changes the order, but the meaning is the same. The sentence flips: "A new battery is what you need." This shows you can reverse Wh-Cleft
narrative: The Hydra holds a heavy car battery in its main head. It moves the battery all the way to its tail. It changes the order, but the meaning is the same. The sentence flips: "A new battery is what you need." This shows you can reverse Wh-Clefts.

context: An Imp paints a big word "IS" on the wall. A big pile of plural nouns falls on him. Even with the heavy weight, he says the verb must be singular. The rule is: The Wh-clause is singular. Even if your noun is plural, use is or was.
narrative: Example: "What they need is more time." (Not "are"—use is even though "they" is plural.)

context: The Jester points at the Imp and laughs. He uses the word "That" to talk about the whole thing. He says: "That's what I'm talking about." This shows you can use "That" to talk about what just happened.
narrative: Go to the last street.

context: A small Kitten sleeps at the bottom of a black stone. It does not want toys or food. It shows that the only thing it wants is rest. It says: "All I want is more sleep." This is the "All" Cleft. Here, "All" means "the only thing."
narrative: A small Kitten sleeps at the bottom of a black stone. It does not want toys or food. It shows that the only thing it wants is rest. It says: "All I want is more sleep." This is the "All" Cleft. Here, "All" means "the only thing."

context: A Lion wears a detective hat. He looks at the ground with a glass. He ignores the police. He tries to do the action himself. "What he did was try to solve the crime himself." The Lion shows the action using "What... do."
narrative: A Lion wears a detective hat. He looks at the ground with a glass. He ignores the police. He tries to do the action himself. "What he did was try to solve the crime himself." The Lion shows the action using "What... do."

context: It holds a red pen and reads a long sentence on a screen. It aggressively crosses out words that are not needed. It explains the definition of this technique.
quote: Ellipsis just means you're deleting words from sentences—unnecessary words or redundant words.
narrative: It holds a red pen and reads a long sentence on a screen. It aggressively crosses out words that are not needed. It explains the definition of this technique.

context: A Neanderthal stands next to the Marmoset holding two mugs. He grunts at a guest. He does not say "Do you want a tea or do you want a coffee?" He just holds them up to save words. He knows that too much talking is bad.
quote: The more words you use in a sentence, the more confusing the sentence gets.
narrative: A Neanderthal stands next to the Marmoset holding two mugs. He grunts at a guest. He does not say "Do you want a tea or do you want a coffee?" He just holds them up to save words. He knows that too much talking is bad.

context: An Owl plays a guitar on the sidewalk. A second Owl watches him. The second Owl does not pick up a guitar, but simply nods to show he can do it too. He avoids repeating the action.
quote: She can play the guitar and he can too.
narrative: An Owl plays a guitar on the sidewalk. A second Owl watches him. The second Owl does not pick up a guitar, but simply nods to show he can do it too. He avoids repeating the action.

context: A black Panther stalks a sentence written on the ground. It pounces on a repeated phrase and swaps it for a decoy word. It explains that this is a specific technique for replacing words.
quote: Substitution is exactly what it says it is: you're substituting words, you're replacing words in a phrase or even part of a phrase as well to avoid repeating the same words.
narrative: A black Panther stalks a sentence written on the ground. It pounces on a repeated phrase and swaps it for a decoy word. It explains that this is a specific technique for replacing words.

context: The feathered serpent Quetzalcoatl wears a mechanic's belt. He coils around a broken sentence engine. He holds a wrench labeled "Auxiliary" in his mouth. He adjusts the "Tense" gear to make sure it corresponds perfectly.
quote: The auxiliary verb needs to correspond with the types of verbs that you're using... it also needs to correspond in tense as well.
narrative: The feathered serpent Quetzalcoatl wears a mechanic's belt. He coils around a broken sentence engine. He holds a wrench labeled "Auxiliary" in his mouth. He adjusts the "Tense" gear to make sure it corresponds perfectly.

context: A Rat looks at a calendar on the wall. Someone says "He will come today." The Rat shakes its head and gnaws on the sentence. It removes the prediction and leaves only the word "it" behind.
quote: He might come today, but I doubt it.
narrative: A Rat looks at a calendar on the wall. Someone says "He will come today." The Rat shakes its head and gnaws on the sentence. It removes the prediction and leaves only the word "it" behind.

context: A floating Skull hovers at the end of the street. It stares at a paragraph full of dead weight. It disintegrates the extra words, leaving only the bare bones of the sentence to make it sleek.
quote: It just makes your writing much more concise and it makes it flow better as well.
narrative: A floating Skull hovers at the end of the street. It stares at a paragraph full of dead weight. It disintegrates the extra words, leaving only the bare bones of the sentence to make it sleek.

context: A colorful Toucan sits on a bench. It is sweating profusely in the sun. It decides to remove its heavy feathers like a coat. It explains the result of the heat.
quote: It was hot, so I took off my jacket.
narrative: A colorful Toucan sits on a bench. It is sweating profusely in the sun. It decides to remove its heavy feathers like a coat. It explains the result of the heat.

narrative: A Unicorn wearing a suit acts as an examiner. It hands a failed exam paper to a student. It explains formally that because of this result, there is no job offer.

quote: We have therefore decided not to offer you the job.

context: A participle clause is a subordinate clause used to give extra information.
The subject of the participle clause and the main clause must be the same.
Present Active (Simultaneous Actions) - Two things happening at the same time.
Present Active (Reason) - Stating a reason before the result.
Present Active (Negative Form) - Place "not" before the participle.
Present Active (Consequence) - Action first, then the result.
Present Active (Ambiguity) - Flip the sentence if the subject is unclear.
Perfect Active (Sequence) - Action fully completed before the main clause.
Past Participle (Subject Info) - Adding information about the subject.
Past Participle (Condition) - Reduced conditional stating a fact.
Perfect Passive (Sequence/Reason) - Passive action completed before main clause.
The Dangling Participle - Subject mismatch.
Definition of Nominalization (turning words into nouns).
Transforming Verbs into Nouns (Enjoy -> Enjoyment).
Transforming Adjectives into Nouns (Beautiful -> Beauty).
The "Noun of Noun" Structure (Develop -> Development).
Advanced Nominalization with Relational Verbs (Leads to).
Core definitions: Prefix (before) and Suffix (after).
Suffix -able indicates ability.
Suffix -ish softens time or adjectives.
Prefix un- means not complete or absent.
Prefix un- can also mean to reverse an action.
Prefix dis- indicates the opposite or active negation.
Prefix mis- refers to a mistake.
Prefixes im-, in-, ir- spelling rules.
Insecure (feeling) vs. Unsecure (safety).
Prefix re- means to repeat.
Spoken language is built from segments: consonants (bricks) and vowels (mortar).
Suprasegmentals are features "beyond the segment" that emerge only through comparison.
Length is the relative duration of a sound.
Stress can alter a word's meaning, pitch, and sound properties.
Intonation is the pitch pattern at the sentence level, which can change meaning.
Linguistically, only the relative values of pitch matter, not the absolute values.
The IPA chart has a dedicated section for suprasegmental symbols.
Thought groups involve using short pauses to break down sentences.
English is a stress-timed language with regular intervals.
Linking occurs when the end of one word blends directly into the start of the next word.
Shadowing is actively repeating a text simultaneously to absorb natural rhythm.
Connected speech involves changing, losing, or adding sounds.
Assimilation is when a sound changes to be more like its neighbor.
Preparing for /b/ by closing lips early changes /n/ to /m/.
Elision is the deletion or loss of sounds.
Final 't' or 'd' sounds are the most commonly lost in English.
Intrusion is the addition of a new sound.
Only 'w', 'y', or 'r' sounds are usually added in intrusion.
Syllabic L [l̩] takes over the entire syllable when the vowel is reduced.
Syllabic N [n̩] frequently occurs after alveolar consonants like /t/ or /s/, often utilizing a glottal stop.
Syllabic M [m̩] acts as its own syllable, often found in words ending in "thm" or "sm".
